title: How to Calculate PAYE and Net Salary in Kenya in 2026
content:
PAYE is income tax withheld by your employer. It is only one deduction on a Kenyan payslip: pension contributions, health contributions and Housing Levy also affect the amount reaching your bank. Start by separating gross cash pay, taxable pay and take-home pay.

1. Establish the pay that is taxable

Add salary and taxable cash allowances. Regular commuter and cash medical allowances are not automatically tax-free. Employer-provided medical cover and properly supported business reimbursements have different rules. Add the correctly valued taxable benefit where an employer provides a car or housing; there is no general rule that all benefits are valued at 30% of salary.

2. Deduct qualifying amounts before calculating tax

For a straightforward salary, subtract employee NSSF, SHIF and employee Housing Levy to obtain taxable pay. Other qualifying deductions can include registered pension contributions, owner-occupied mortgage interest and post-retirement medical fund contributions, subject to their limits. Do not subtract the employer’s NSSF or Housing Levy share from the employee’s salary.

3. Apply the progressive bands

Monthly taxable pay sliceRate
First 24,00010%
Next 8,33325%
Next 467,667 (up to 500,000)30%
Next 300,000 (up to 800,000)32.5%
Amount above 800,00035%

These are slices of taxable income. A salary entering the 30% band does not make the first two slices taxable at 30%. KRA lists these bands as effective from July 2023; calling them the rates used in 2026 does not mean new bands were introduced in 2026.

4. Apply relief after calculating tax

A qualifying resident employee receives KES 2,400 monthly personal relief. Subtract applicable insurance relief at this stage too. Relief reduces the calculated tax, whereas a deduction reduces taxable income. PAYE cannot become negative merely because relief exceeds the tax.

Worked example: KES 100,000 gross

Examples use a resident employee with one job, regular monthly cash pay, pensionable pay equal to gross pay, the February 2026 NSSF limits and standard personal relief. They exclude benefits in kind, voluntary pension contributions, mortgage interest, insurance relief, disability exemptions, HELB and other personal deductions. Figures are in KES; payroll rounding can produce small differences.

ItemMonthly KES
Gross salary100,000.00
Employee NSSF6,000.00
SHIF2,750.00
Employee Housing Levy1,500.00
Taxable pay89,750.00
PAYE after personal relief19,308.35
Take-home pay70,441.65

Taxable pay is KES 89,750. Tax before relief is KES 2,400 + KES 2,083.25 + KES 17,225.10 = KES 21,708.35. Subtract KES 2,400 personal relief to obtain PAYE of KES 19,308.35. The resulting take-home pay is KES 70,441.65.

5. Reconcile the cash received

Take-home pay equals gross cash salary less employee NSSF, SHIF, Housing Levy, PAYE and any authorised personal deductions. A non-cash benefit can increase PAYE without adding cash to the bank payment. HELB or a salary advance reduces cash received but does not automatically reduce taxable income.

What changes for higher earners?

Only taxable pay above KES 500,000 enters the 32.5% slice; only the amount above KES 800,000 enters the 35% slice. Employee NSSF stops increasing at its earnings ceiling, but SHIF and Housing Levy do not share that ceiling. Compare incremental net pay when negotiating a raise, rather than multiplying the whole salary by the highest rate.

title: NSSF Contributions in Kenya: 2026 Rates and Take-Home Impact
content:
The Year 4 NSSF contribution limits apply from February 2026. Employees contribute 6% of pensionable pay within the statutory ceiling and employers contribute an equal amount. The maximum of KES 12,960 in the official notice is the combined employee and employer amount, not the amount to deduct from one employee.

The two tiers

TierPensionable payEmployee maximumEmployer maximum
IFirst 9,000540540
IIAbove 9,000 up to 108,0005,9405,940
CombinedUp to 108,0006,4806,480

For pay below KES 9,000, use 6% of actual pensionable earnings rather than a flat KES 540. Tier II is 6% of the earnings above KES 9,000, limited to KES 99,000. The upper earnings limit is the total ceiling, not an extra band to add above it.

Examples

Pensionable payEmployee contributionEmployer contribution
9,000540540
30,0001,8001,800
50,0003,0003,000
72,0004,3204,320
100,0006,0006,000
108,0006,4806,480
150,0006,4806,480

Who pays more than in January 2026?

Year 3 used an upper earnings limit of KES 72,000 and a maximum employee contribution of KES 4,320. Raising the ceiling affects employees above KES 72,000. Someone on KES 50,000 still contributes KES 3,000: changing the boundary between tiers does not change the combined 6% at that salary.

At KES 100,000, employee NSSF rises by KES 1,680, from KES 4,320 to KES 6,000. Where the extra pension deduction reduces income taxed at 30%, PAYE falls by KES 504 and take-home falls by KES 1,176. The employer’s own cost rises by the full KES 1,680. These are different effects.

Payroll checks

Check pensionable earnings, contribution period, Tier I and Tier II amounts, and the employer match. A qualifying contracted-out Tier II arrangement needs the appropriate approval; an ordinary savings account is not a substitute. Do not assume pensionable pay is always basic salary plus an invented fixed percentage of housing allowance.

The February 2026 NSSF notice requires remittance by the 9th of the following month. Reconcile your member statement with payslip deductions and raise missing credits with payroll. When comparing annual earnings, keep January separate from February onwards.

title: SHIF Deductions in Kenya: SHA Rates and PAYE Treatment
content:
SHA is the Social Health Authority; SHIF is the Social Health Insurance Fund it administers. They are not two separate payroll deductions. The current SHA premium page sets salaried contributions at 2.75% of gross monthly income, with a KES 300 minimum and no upper ceiling.

Calculate the monthly deduction

Gross monthly incomeSHIF contribution
10,000300 (minimum)
30,000825
50,0001,375
100,0002,750
200,0005,500

For this simple salaried calculation, take the larger of KES 300 and gross monthly income multiplied by 0.0275. Do not apply the NSSF earnings ceiling to SHIF. An employee earning above KES 108,000 continues to pay SHIF on the applicable gross income.

How SHIF affects PAYE

KRA lists employee SHIF contributions as an allowable deduction from employment income. That lowers taxable pay before the PAYE bands are applied. It is not an extra 15% insurance-relief credit: applying both treatments to the same contribution would overstate the relief.

For example, a KES 2,750 SHIF deduction lowers PAYE by KES 825 if the full deduction falls within the 30% band. Its net cash cost in that example is KES 1,925. The actual saving depends on the person’s taxable income and other deductions; it is not a universal rebate.

What happened to NHIF?

The transition to the SHA system began in October 2024. An old NHIF income-band table should not be used to calculate a current SHIF salary deduction. When reviewing an older payslip, use the system and tax treatment applicable to that period rather than rewriting it using today’s rules.

Employment and household assessment are different

Employers calculate and remit salaried deductions to SHA. For non-salaried households, SHA uses a means-testing process to assess household income. A salary calculator is not a substitute for that assessment, nor does paying a contribution mean every procedure at every hospital is covered.

Check your account and cover

Match the deduction to your payslip, verify your registration and contribution record using the official SHA member service, and check the contracted facility and benefit tariff before treatment. If a deduction is missing from your account, ask payroll for its remittance evidence. Do not infer a contribution holiday from an old headline about court proceedings.

title: Housing Levy in Kenya: Calculation, PAYE and Employer Duties
content:
Under the Affordable Housing Act 2024 collection framework, an employee and employer each contribute 1.5% of the employee’s gross monthly salary. Only the employee’s share comes out of the employee’s pay. The employer funds its own share separately.

Salary examples

Monthly salaryEmployee 1.5%Employer 1.5%Total remitted
20,000300300600
50,0007507501,500
100,0001,5001,5003,000
200,0003,0003,0006,000

These examples assume ordinary regular cash salary. The levy has no NSSF-style earnings ceiling. At KES 100,000, deducting the combined KES 3,000 from the employee would incorrectly charge them the employer’s share.

Use the correct pay base

KRA’s gross-salary clarification includes basic salary and regular cash allowances. It distinguishes these from non-cash benefits and irregular payments such as a one-off bonus or terminal dues. Classification matters: a payment can be taxable for PAYE without automatically belonging in the Housing Levy base. Ask payroll to explain the treatment of unusual or recurring bonus arrangements.

The current PAYE deduction

KRA’s current PAYE guidance includes employee Housing Levy among deductions used to arrive at taxable employment income. Do not also apply the old Affordable Housing Relief as an extra tax credit. Older notices describe the historical relief, so their rate and collection details must be read alongside subsequent tax changes.

At a 30% marginal PAYE rate, a KES 1,500 allowable deduction reduces PAYE by KES 450 if the whole deduction falls in that band. The levy still costs the employee money; it is not fully refunded through PAYE.

Payment deadline and evidence

KRA specifies the ninth working day after the end of the month. This differs from PAYE’s ninth calendar day. The employer should reconcile the levy schedule, its own contribution and payment confirmation rather than assume paying PAYE has settled the levy too. The 2024 collection notice describes a 3% monthly penalty on unpaid levy; it does not say 1% daily interest.

What the levy does not mean

A payslip contribution is not proof that a house has been allocated to you, nor is it a personal savings balance that can automatically be withdrawn on leaving employment. Use the official housing programme’s separate eligibility and allocation process. Non-employment income has its own levy obligations; the salary examples above do not determine every business case.

title: Net to Gross Salary in Kenya: How to Work Backwards
content:
A net salary target cannot reliably be converted to gross pay by adding a fixed percentage. PAYE is progressive, NSSF has a ceiling and your personal deductions may differ from a colleague’s. The practical method is to test a gross figure, calculate its deductions and adjust it until the net result matches your target.

Agree what “net” includes

Ask whether the offer means net after statutory deductions only or after HELB, a staff loan, voluntary pension and insurance premiums too. Also distinguish a cash salary from a package including employer pension contributions or a company car. A company car can add taxable value without providing cash to meet your target.

Calculate each candidate gross salary

For a standard resident salary, calculate employee NSSF, SHIF and Housing Levy; subtract allowable deductions to get taxable pay; apply the PAYE bands and reliefs; then subtract the actual payroll deductions from cash gross. Repeat with a higher or lower candidate salary. The net-to-gross calculator helps perform that iteration.

Examples use a resident employee with one job, regular monthly cash pay, pensionable pay equal to gross pay, the February 2026 NSSF limits and standard personal relief. They exclude benefits in kind, voluntary pension contributions, mortgage interest, insurance relief, disability exemptions, HELB and other personal deductions. Figures are in KES; payroll rounding can produce small differences.

A useful reference point

ItemMonthly KES
Gross salary100,000.00
Employee NSSF6,000.00
SHIF2,750.00
Employee Housing Levy1,500.00
Taxable pay89,750.00
PAYE after personal relief19,308.35
Take-home pay70,441.65

With these assumptions, KES 100,000 gross produces KES 70,441.65 net. A KES 70,000 target therefore needs slightly less than KES 100,000 gross. It does not need KES 70,000 plus 30%: that approach would ignore the different deduction bases and progressive bands.

Why the result changes at different salaries

Below the NSSF ceiling, extra pensionable salary can increase the pension deduction. Above it, the employee’s mandatory NSSF is capped. SHIF and Housing Levy continue increasing with the applicable pay. A move into a higher tax band affects only the next slice of taxable income, not the whole salary.

Avoid common negotiation mistakes

Specify monthly or annual amounts and the tax period. Use resident status correctly and include evidence-backed reliefs only. If your employer pays a guaranteed net amount, ask who bears future statutory changes and how bonus months are handled. Review the first payslip against the agreed calculation and retain it with the offer letter.

See the full PAYE method for the underlying bands. Estimates for 2026 should not be presented as guaranteed 2027 payroll results.

title: Legal Ways to Reduce PAYE in Kenya: Deductions and Reliefs
content:
The safest way to avoid paying too much PAYE is to make sure payroll has applied deductions and reliefs you actually qualify for. Buying an unnecessary policy or locking away money solely for a tax saving can leave you with less usable cash.

Deduction or relief?

A deduction reduces taxable income before the bands are applied. A relief reduces the resulting tax. A KES 10,000 deduction may save KES 3,000 where it all falls in the 30% band; a KES 1,500 relief reduces tax by KES 1,500, subject to the tax available to offset.

Check these items on your payslip

  • Resident personal relief: KES 2,400 per month.
  • Employee SHIF and Housing Levy: allowable deductions, not additional insurance or housing tax credits.
  • Registered pension contributions, including NSSF: subject to the pension deduction limits.
  • Qualifying owner-occupied mortgage interest: interest rather than the entire loan repayment.
  • Qualifying life, health or education insurance premiums: insurance relief subject to policy and statutory conditions.
  • Post-retirement medical fund contributions: a separate allowable deduction subject to its limit.
  • A valid disability income-tax exemption certificate, where applicable.

Provide evidence before payroll closes

Send policy certificates, premium statements, mortgage interest statements, registered scheme details and any exemption certificate to payroll. KRA’s employer guidance requires relevant supported deductions and reliefs to be applied. A verbal request or an unregistered savings arrangement is not enough.

Avoid false “tax hacks”

Renaming a cash allowance does not make it tax-free. Ordinary commuting, rent, school fees and personal loan repayments do not automatically become employee income-tax deductions. A SACCO deposit is not the same as a contribution to a registered pension scheme. Do not claim an expense twice through payroll and again as if payroll had never recognised it.

Families and shared costs

Marriage does not create a general dependent-spouse PAYE credit or allow arbitrary transfers of unused personal relief. Where a qualifying policy covers a family member, establish who paid and who is entitled to claim; do not claim the same premium twice. Joint property ownership alone does not establish entitlement to deduct the whole mortgage interest. For mixed spousal business or investment income, check the applicable return rules with KRA rather than using a salary illustration as filing advice.

Compare the cash impact

An extra pension contribution can reduce tax while also reducing take-home pay because the contribution goes into retirement savings. Choose the contribution with your budget and access needs in mind. The detailed guides to insurance relief, mortgage interest and pensions show the differences.

title: Insurance Relief in Kenya: The 15% Rule and KES 60,000 Cap
content:
The KES 60,000 annual limit is the maximum insurance tax relief, not the maximum premium you may pay. Confusing those two amounts substantially understates the relief. The monthly relief cap is KES 5,000.

Calculate the relief

Qualifying annual premiums15% of premiumsAnnual relief before tax-liability limit
30,0004,5004,500
60,0009,0009,000
120,00018,00018,000
400,00060,00060,000
500,00075,00060,000

The formula is the smaller of 15% of qualifying premiums and KES 60,000 annually. A KES 10,000 qualifying monthly premium produces KES 1,500 monthly relief. Do not then multiply that relief by your marginal tax rate: it reduces the calculated tax itself.

Which policies can qualify?

KRA identifies qualifying life, health and education policies for the taxpayer and eligible family members. Education policies require a maturity period of at least ten years. Ask the insurer for the tax certificate and check that the policy and payment qualify; a product’s marketing label is not proof of entitlement.

Do not assume motor, household or travel cover qualifies simply because it is insurance. Nor should you claim employee relief on a premium you did not bear. Employer-provided medical cover has its own treatment and should not be confused with a cash medical allowance.

SHIF is different

Employee SHIF contributions are deducted in arriving at taxable employment income under the current rules. Do not enter the same SHIF payment as qualifying private insurance premiums and claim a second benefit.

How to claim through payroll

Give payroll the policy details, premium evidence and insurer’s tax certificate. Check the relief appears after tax has been calculated. Keep those records for the annual reconciliation and check that the year’s premium amount agrees with what you actually paid. Annual lump-sum premiums need correct allocation; do not invent monthly payments to fit the cap.

If you missed the claim

Compare the insurer’s certificate, your P9 and payroll records before seeking a correction or refund. An unused allowance does not automatically produce a cash payment when there is no tax to offset. Do not cancel and replace cover purely to chase the headline maximum: compare the policy’s protection, exclusions, premium and affordability.

title: Mortgage Interest Tax Deduction in Kenya: Limits and Eligibility
content:
Qualifying mortgage interest reduces taxable income. It is not a refund of the mortgage repayment and it does not mean KRA pays KES 30,000 towards your mortgage each month. The current limit is KES 360,000 per year, equivalent to KES 30,000 per month.

Check the property and lender

KRA describes the deduction for borrowing from qualifying institutions specified in the Income Tax Act to purchase or improve premises occupied by the borrower for residential purposes. Confirm both the loan purpose and lender qualification. Do not assume every SACCO, private lender, land loan or rental investment qualifies.

Separate interest from capital

Use a lender statement showing the interest actually charged and paid for the relevant period. If the payment is KES 50,000 but only KES 28,000 is qualifying interest, the starting deduction is KES 28,000, not KES 50,000. Principal repayments reduce your debt but are not mortgage interest.

Qualifying monthly interestDeduction within the monthly capIllustrative saving at 30%
20,00020,0006,000
28,00028,0008,400
40,00030,0009,000

These savings assume the whole deduction falls in the 30% band and enough taxable income is available. A deduction crossing bands produces a different result. KES 9,000 is therefore an example, not a universal maximum tax saving for every earner.

Documents for payroll

Provide the loan agreement, lender interest statement and evidence supporting owner occupation and the loan’s purpose. For joint borrowing, explain ownership, liability and who paid the interest. Two borrowers should not each claim the full interest on the same payment.

A practical payslip check

Find the mortgage deduction in the calculation of taxable pay, before PAYE is calculated. Check that it has not also been entered as a separate tax credit. If you pay the lender directly, do not subtract the payment again from payslip cash unless payroll actually collected it. Taxable-pay deductions and cash deductions are different entries.

Review the year as a whole

Retain the annual lender certificate and reconcile monthly claims against it. If interest changes during the year, update payroll. Use the rules applying to the year of income when correcting an older return rather than applying today’s limit retrospectively.

title: Pension Contributions and PAYE in Kenya: Tax Savings and Trade-Offs
content:
Contributing to a registered pension can reduce PAYE, but “everyone should max it out” is poor advice. You also need money for current bills, debt payments and emergencies. A pension contribution moves cash into retirement savings; the tax saving covers only part of the contribution.

The deduction limit

Qualifying contributions to registered retirement arrangements are subject to the statutory deduction rules, including the KES 30,000 monthly / KES 360,000 annual ceiling. The allowable employee contribution is also limited by the actual contribution and the applicable 30% pensionable-income test. NSSF uses part of the available pension deduction; it is not an extra KES 30,000 allowance on top of a full separate NSSF deduction.

Example: extra savings on a KES 100,000 salary

Under the standard February 2026 assumptions, mandatory employee NSSF is KES 6,000. If an additional KES 10,000 registered pension contribution qualifies and is fully deductible within the limits, PAYE falls by KES 3,000 where the whole deduction is in the 30% band. Take-home falls by KES 7,000 while KES 10,000 goes into pension savings. It does not increase take-home by KES 3,000.

Check scheme registration and costs

Confirm the scheme’s registration, charges, investment approach and access rules. Ordinary savings, shares or SACCO deposits are not automatically registered pension contributions. Ask the scheme for written details and statements rather than relying on a promised return or a provider ranking.

Employer contributions are separate

Your employer’s statutory NSSF match is an additional employer cost. It should not be taken out of your cash salary. Employer pension contributions and contributions made under special employer arrangements have their own tax conditions; do not simply copy an employee deduction calculation.

What to send payroll

Provide the registered scheme details, the contribution instruction and evidence of actual contributions. Reconcile contributions shown on the payslip with those credited to the scheme. If an annual contribution is made outside payroll, keep the statement for tax reconciliation and check the annual limit rather than assuming every payment is fully deductible.

Choose an affordable contribution

Compare the extra retirement savings with the reduction in usable monthly cash. Decide how much liquidity you need before increasing deductions. Tax rules on withdrawals depend on the type of benefit, membership and retirement circumstances, so the tax deduction at contribution stage is not a blanket promise that every withdrawal will be tax-free.

title: Income Tax Exemption for Persons with Disability in Kenya
content:
KRA’s published administrative guidance provides for exemption on the first KES 150,000 of total monthly income, or KES 1.8 million annually, for an eligible person with disability. Registration with NCPWD and a valid income-tax exemption certificate matter: a disability card alone is not the same as payroll approval to exempt income.

Start with the certificate

Check the certificate’s validity dates, the income covered and any conditions. Give payroll a copy before asking for the exemption to be applied. If a renewal is needed, use the current NCPWD and KRA process and retain your application evidence. Do not assume a pending application automatically extends an expired certificate.

How the limit works

The published KES 150,000 figure is exempt income, not a KES 150,000 credit against tax. Income above the exemption must be assessed under the applicable rules. The exemption is personal: splitting earnings between employers does not multiply the annual allowance.

Other payroll deductions

An income-tax exemption does not, by itself, remove every non-tax deduction on a payslip. NSSF, SHIF, Housing Levy and loan deductions have their own rules. Ask payroll to separate the PAYE calculation from each other contribution and show the legal basis for any exemption it applies.

Check records before filing

Reconcile the P9, certificate dates, income from each source and tax already withheld. If payroll began applying the certificate partway through a year, establish its effective date before claiming an earlier-period adjustment. Do not claim the same exempt income separately against each job.

Where the guidance and your circumstances differ

Disability legislation and administrative implementation can change. This article reports KRA’s published certificate-based treatment checked for this review; it should not be read as limiting any wider statutory entitlement. If your certificate, a newer legal provision or KRA’s instructions differ, obtain a written determination for your circumstances rather than substituting a generic calculator.

title: KES 50,000 Salary After Tax in Kenya (2026)
content:
A regular gross salary of KES 50,000 produces estimated take-home pay of KES 39,029.15 per month under the assumptions below. PAYE is KES 5,845.85; the remainder of the difference between gross and net consists of employee NSSF, SHIF and Housing Levy.

Examples use a resident employee with one job, regular monthly cash pay, pensionable pay equal to gross pay, the February 2026 NSSF limits and standard personal relief. They exclude benefits in kind, voluntary pension contributions, mortgage interest, insurance relief, disability exemptions, HELB and other personal deductions. Figures are in KES; payroll rounding can produce small differences.

Monthly payslip breakdown

ItemMonthly KES
Gross salary50,000.00
Employee NSSF3,000.00
SHIF1,375.00
Employee Housing Levy750.00
Taxable pay44,875.00
PAYE after personal relief5,845.85
Take-home pay39,029.15

How the PAYE figure is calculated

Subtract employee NSSF of KES 3,000.00, SHIF of KES 1,375.00 and Housing Levy of KES 750.00 from gross pay. This leaves KES 44,875.00 taxable income. Apply 10% to the first KES 24,000, 25% to the next KES 8,333 and 30% to the remaining KES 12,542.00. Subtract KES 2,400 resident personal relief after calculating tax.

The NSSF detail that matters at this salary

At this salary, NSSF is KES 3,000 rather than the maximum KES 6,480. The February 2026 increase in the ceiling does not increase the total contribution on KES 50,000 pensionable pay. Applying the maximum to every employee would understate take-home pay.

Why your bank payment may differ

A voluntary pension contribution, qualifying mortgage interest or insurance relief can change PAYE. A company car or employer-provided housing can add taxable value without adding cash. HELB repayments, a staff loan or authorised deductions can reduce the bank payment further. Compare each payslip line rather than treating every difference as an incorrect tax rate.

For a non-resident employee, do not assume resident personal relief applies. A valid disability exemption also changes the calculation. If the stated salary is basic pay and allowances are paid on top, use the total applicable cash earnings rather than this basic-pay figure alone.

Budget from the net amount

Use KES 39,029.15 as the starting point only if these assumptions match your employment. Subtract commitments paid outside payroll, such as rent and loan instalments, to find what is available for day-to-day spending and savings. Employer NSSF of KES 3,000.00 and employer Housing Levy of KES 750.00 are not part of this cash budget.

Annual figures need the right periods

Multiplying one monthly estimate by twelve is only an illustration. January 2026 used the earlier NSSF ceiling, and bonuses, job changes and varying reliefs can affect the actual annual result. Use the year’s payroll records and P9 for a return rather than twelve identical estimates.

Use the interactive KES 50,000 breakdown or the full PAYE explanation to check your inputs.

title: Bonus and 13th-Month Pay Tax in Kenya
content:
A bonus or 13th-month salary is generally employment income for PAYE. There is no universal separate “bonus tax rate”, and a collective bargaining agreement does not itself create an income-tax exemption. The correct result depends on the income period, the employee’s other pay and the payment’s classification.

What changes in a bonus month?

The taxable bonus increases employment income. In a simple current-period calculation, compare tax on ordinary taxable pay with tax after adding the bonus; the difference is the additional PAYE. Where all the extra taxable amount stays in the 30% slice, an extra KES 10,000 of taxable income adds KES 3,000 PAYE. Crossing a band boundary changes the rate on only the slice above it.

Do not duplicate personal relief

Personal relief is not granted again because salary and bonus are paid separately. Use the combined payroll calculation and the correct tax period. Tax withheld is reconciled against the year’s liability; a bonus does not automatically entitle you to a refund.

Past-service bonuses and arrears

Payments relating to earlier periods can require allocation under KRA’s lump-sum guidance rather than a crude multiplication of one month’s tax. Ask payroll which period the payment relates to and request its calculation. Historical examples in the older KRA guidance explain allocation but use old tax bands; they are not current-rate calculators.

Check contributions separately

A PAYE-taxable payment is not automatically treated identically for NSSF, SHIF and Housing Levy. KRA’s Housing Levy clarification excludes irregular payments such as one-off bonuses from the gross monthly salary definition. A regular contractual payment requires classification based on its substance. NSSF depends on pensionable pay and the ceiling; use the relevant scheme rules rather than blindly adding every deduction percentage.

What to request from payroll

  • The gross bonus and period earned.
  • The ordinary and bonus-inclusive taxable pay calculations.
  • The treatment under each statutory contribution.
  • Reliefs already used in the period.
  • The net cash bonus and supporting payslip.

A contractual 13th-month payment and a discretionary performance bonus may have different employment entitlements even where both are taxable. Read your contract or collective agreement for the entitlement, then apply the tax rules separately.

title: Freelancing vs Employment in Kenya: Compare Tax and Real Income
content:
Freelancing is not automatically taxed less than employment. Compare salary with profit after genuine business costs, not with the total value of invoices. A contractor also funds downtime, equipment, retirement savings and other costs an employer may cover.

Employee income

An employer deducts PAYE from employment income and accounts for the relevant payroll contributions. A salary offer may also include employer-funded pension contributions, paid leave or medical cover. Those benefits matter when comparing a job with an invoice rate.

Freelance business income

A sole trader generally accounts for taxable business income under the individual income-tax rules, with allowable business expenses supported by records. This is not a blanket 30% tax on every freelancer’s turnover. Personal costs do not become deductible merely because they are paid from the business bank account.

Withholding tax is not always the final bill

Where a client deducts non-final withholding tax, obtain the certificate and reconcile it with the annual liability. Do not assume that a percentage withheld by a client settles all tax on your business profit. The treatment depends on the income type, residence and applicable rules.

Do not assume turnover tax applies

KRA’s turnover-tax regime covers eligible resident businesses above KES 1 million and up to KES 25 million annual turnover, but expressly excludes management, professional and training fees, among other income. A professional freelancer should not choose turnover tax simply because the headline 1.5% appears cheaper.

Where turnover tax does apply, it is on gross sales with no expense deduction. A low-margin business can therefore face a significant tax cost relative to profit. VAT, invoicing and other obligations must be considered separately; turnover tax does not cancel them.

Build a like-for-like comparison

Employment offerFreelance equivalent to budget
Monthly gross salaryRevenue less genuine business costs
Paid leaveUnbilled weeks
Employer pension contributionSelf-funded retirement provision
Employer equipmentEquipment, maintenance and software
Predictable payrollLate payment and bad-debt exposure

For illustration, KES 100,000 invoiced less KES 25,000 business costs leaves KES 75,000 before personal taxes and contributions. It is not equivalent to a KES 100,000 salary. Keep a reserve for taxes using your actual regime and cashflow, not an unsupported universal percentage.

Records and filing

Keep invoices, receipts, payment records and withholding certificates. The annual return may need both employment and business income if you do both. Check the filing-deadline guide for the 2027 change and keep the two income streams identifiable in your records.

title: HELB Salary Deductions: What Employees and Employers Should Check
content:
HELB repayments are loan repayments. They reduce the amount you receive, but they are not a general deduction from taxable salary for PAYE. Your employer should use the repayment details supplied through HELB’s employer process, not an assumed universal percentage of salary.

How the amount is established

HELB directs employers to disclose staff and obtain the outstanding balance and monthly deduction rate through its employer portal. Borrowers can check their own loan statement. Do not rely on an unofficial table claiming that every graduate starts repayment at the same salary threshold or pays the same percentage.

The employer’s monthly task

The employer deducts the instructed amount, submits the deduction information and remits it to HELB. HELB’s employer portal guidance specifies the 15th day of the following month. This is a separate obligation from paying PAYE to KRA; entering a deduction in payroll does not prove HELB has received it.

Example of the cash effect

If take-home before HELB is KES 70,441.65 and the instructed repayment is KES 5,000, the resulting bank payment is KES 65,441.65, assuming no other deductions. PAYE does not fall by treating that KES 5,000 as pension or mortgage interest. The loan balance should reflect the amount actually credited by HELB.

Check more than the payslip

  1. Compare the payroll deduction with the current HELB instruction.
  2. Check the same period in your HELB statement.
  3. If a credit is missing, request the employer’s remittance reference and schedule.
  4. Raise an unmatched payment with HELB using the reference and borrower details.
  5. Keep the correspondence until the statement has been corrected.

When you change jobs or finish repayment

Tell the new employer about the loan and use HELB’s current process to establish the amount due. Near settlement, obtain an up-to-date balance and arrange confirmation of clearance and deduction stoppage. Do not stop repayments solely because your own spreadsheet reaches zero: interest, prior unmatched payments or adjustments may affect the balance.

If the repayment is unaffordable

Contact HELB about your situation and request a documented arrangement. Neither a blog nor an informal agreement with payroll changes the lender’s instruction automatically. Avoid sending payments using old account details copied from third-party articles; follow HELB’s current official payment instructions.

title: Changing Jobs in Kenya: PAYE, P9s and Overlapping Pay
content:
Changing employers does not reset your annual income-tax history. Each payroll accounts for the employment income it pays; your annual reconciliation must reflect the relevant income and tax from both jobs.

Before you leave

Keep your final payslip, employment dates, details of any bonus or terminal payment, and the P9 for that employer when available. Ask payroll to explain notice pay, unused leave, gratuity and any adjustments separately. A single “final settlement” line can conceal different tax treatments.

Give the new payroll accurate information

Supply the correct KRA PIN and the documents supporting relevant deductions and reliefs. Check bank details, pension membership and any HELB instruction too. Do not assume a policy certificate or disability exemption held by the old employer has automatically reached the new one.

When two employers pay in the same month

An overlapping month can lead to duplicated personal relief or deductions based on two separate sets of bands. Tell payroll about the overlap and ask how it will be handled. You are not entitled to two personal-relief allowances for the same period just because two employers pay you.

A gap between jobs

A gap can change the annual tax position, but it does not guarantee a refund. Other income, terminal dues and relief allocation affect the outcome. Reconcile the whole calendar year using actual figures, rather than annualising only the new salary.

The annual reconciliation

  1. Collect the P9 from each employer and check your PIN.
  2. Match the employment periods and income to payslips.
  3. Identify duplicated or omitted reliefs and contributions.
  4. Check taxable benefits and terminal payments.
  5. Reconcile tax withheld with the annual return and correct discrepancies.

The employer’s monthly PAYE return is different from your individual annual return. See current filing deadlines for the change taking effect from January 2027.

If the numbers do not match

Ask the relevant payroll team for a written calculation and corrected supporting records. Retain both the original and corrected documents. Where an employer has deducted tax but the credit does not appear as expected, raise the evidence with KRA rather than simply paying it again or omitting the income.

title: Wrong PAYE Deducted in Kenya? How to Check and Correct It
content:
A lower-than-expected bank payment does not necessarily mean PAYE is wrong. First separate income tax from NSSF, SHIF, Housing Levy, HELB and other deductions. Then reproduce the tax calculation for the relevant month.

Build a clear comparison

Use the same gross earnings, taxable benefits, pensionable pay, residence status and period as payroll. Apply supported deductions before the bands and reliefs after the calculated tax. Check for a bonus, arrears or a benefit that has increased taxable pay without increasing cash salary.

Common mistakes include using an old NSSF ceiling, treating SHIF as insurance relief, granting personal relief twice across jobs, taking both shares of an employer contribution from the employee, or ignoring an eligible documented deduction.

Ask payroll for the calculation

Send a specific query: identify the month, payslip line, amount shown and amount you calculate, and attach the supporting evidence. Ask for the taxable-pay calculation rather than just the bank-payment total. A few cents can be rounding; a repeated material difference needs investigation.

If payroll confirms an error

Request the corrected payslip and, where needed, corrected employer return and P9. Keep a record of the correction and how the difference will be refunded, credited or recovered. Do not assume editing a payslip alone changes a return already filed with KRA.

If tax was overpaid in an earlier year

Reconcile the annual return, tax credits and documentary support before making a refund or offset request through KRA’s official process. A credit balance does not mean an automatic immediate bank payment. KRA may verify the claim and account for outstanding liabilities. Check the current claim window and requirements for the particular tax period rather than relying on a promised processing time.

If payroll cannot resolve it

Use KRA’s official contact or tax-station service with the payslips, P9, calculation and correspondence. If you receive an assessment or formal decision, check the applicable objection deadline promptly; an informal support complaint should not be assumed to preserve a statutory right of objection.

Protect the evidence

Retain receipts, policy certificates and scheme statements supporting reliefs. Do not provide account passwords or one-time codes to someone offering a guaranteed refund. A genuine correction should leave an audit trail from payroll to the return and tax account.

title: The Cost of Hiring an Employee in Kenya: Payroll and Contributions
content:
The cost of employing someone starts with gross salary, not take-home pay. PAYE and employee contributions are usually withheld from that gross salary. Adding them again on top of gross would double-count them.

Employer additions to the salary

Budget the employer’s NSSF contribution and its Housing Levy share separately. Under the February 2026 NSSF limits, the employer matches the employee contribution up to KES 6,480 per month. Housing Levy is 1.5% of the applicable gross monthly salary. SHIF is not a second matching employer contribution simply because payroll remits it.

Illustration for ordinary monthly salary

The KES 107,500 subtotal for a KES 100,000 employee is not an all-in employment budget. It excludes any applicable training levy, insurance, equipment, benefits and contractual or termination costs. Use the employer’s actual obligations rather than a universal “25–40% extra” estimate.

Other items to budget explicitly

  • Applicable NITA levy and work-injury insurance obligations.
  • Contractual pension or medical benefits beyond statutory contributions.
  • Recruitment, onboarding, equipment and software.
  • Cover during leave, overtime and any contractual bonus.
  • Notice, accrued benefits and other lawful exit obligations where relevant.

Paid annual leave is already included in a monthly salary where that salary continues through leave. Add replacement cover if needed, not another full salary charge for the same days. Not every departure creates the same severance entitlement.

Monthly compliance checklist

Register and maintain the relevant employer obligations. Verify employee identifiers, calculate the employee deductions and employer contributions, reconcile the payroll register, file the correct returns and retain payment evidence. PAYE and NSSF are due by the 9th of the following month; Housing Levy uses the ninth working day. Track each obligation separately.

Cashflow and reporting

Reconcile the sum of bank payments and withheld deductions back to gross salary. Then add the employer-funded amounts to reconcile the full cash requirement. Review member credits where relevant: an amount shown as deducted has not necessarily been remitted successfully.

title: Filing PAYE Returns on iTax: Employer Deadline and Checks
content:
An employer’s PAYE return and the PAYE payment are due by the 9th of the following month. The deadline is not the 20th. Filing the return and paying the liability are separate steps; completing one does not automatically complete the other.

Prepare the payroll records

Confirm employee PINs, cash earnings, taxable benefits, allowable deductions and tax reliefs. Reconcile taxable pay and PAYE across the payroll register. Review joiners, leavers, bonuses and any prior-period corrections. Obtain the documentation behind mortgage, insurance, pension and exemption claims before applying them.

Use the current official return process

  1. Open the official iTax service and sign in using the employer account.
  2. Select the PAYE return obligation and the correct monthly period.
  3. Use the current return template or filing workflow offered by KRA.
  4. Validate the figures and resolve errors before submission.
  5. Submit and retain the acknowledgement.
  6. Generate the appropriate payment reference, pay through a supported channel and confirm allocation.

KRA has updated the return process over time. Follow the current template and instructions rather than an article’s old screenshots or invented button names. A P9 is the employee tax record; it is not a replacement for the employer’s monthly PAYE return.

Check the deductions in the right order

Subtract qualifying deductions to arrive at taxable income; apply the progressive tax bands; then apply personal and other eligible reliefs. Do not subtract personal relief from gross pay as if it were a pension contribution. Check the return agrees with what payroll actually deducted.

Nil returns and other obligations

KRA requires a nil PAYE return where there is no PAYE to declare under an active obligation. Separately reconcile SHIF, NSSF, Housing Levy and other required employer payments. PAYE’s ninth-day deadline should not be confused with Housing Levy’s ninth working day.

Late filing and payment

KRA lists late filing at the higher of 25% of tax due and KES 10,000. Late payment attracts a 5% penalty and interest of 1% per month or part-month on unpaid tax. This is not daily 1% interest. If a notice is raised, reconcile the period and liability with KRA and check any applicable relief or amnesty conditions rather than assuming penalties disappear automatically.

Keep a complete trail

Save the payroll register, submitted return, acknowledgement, payment reference and payment confirmation. Review the tax ledger for unmatched amounts. If the submission was wrong, use the formal correction process and retain both versions so employees’ P9s and annual returns remain reconcilable.

title: Taxable Benefits in Kind in Kenya: Cars, Housing and Payroll
content:
A benefit in kind is value received through employment without the equivalent cash being paid into your account. It can increase taxable income and PAYE. That does not mean payroll should subtract the entire benefit value from cash salary as well as deducting its tax.

Start by classifying the payment

Cash allowances and non-cash benefits are different. A cash commuter or medical allowance is not automatically exempt. Employer-provided medical cover has separate treatment. Supported business reimbursements also need to be distinguished from personal expenses paid by an employer.

Company cars

For an employer-owned car, the standard monthly valuation compares 2% of the initial cost with the prescribed value and uses the higher figure. Leased vehicles and restricted private use require the applicable specific treatment. Do not replace this with a made-up annual 4%, 5% or 6% engine-size rule.

For an owned car costing KES 3 million, the 2% calculation is KES 60,000 per month. That is the starting benefit value for the comparison, not KES 60,000 tax. If the final additional taxable benefit is KES 60,000 and all of it lies in a 30% tax slice, the extra PAYE is KES 18,000.

Employer housing

Housing valuation depends on factors including the employee category, remuneration and rent or rental value under the statutory rules. Directors and agricultural employees can have specific treatment. There is no universal KES 36,000 “Nairobi executive” valuation. Ask payroll to show the applicable rule, the underlying figures and any employee payment taken into account.

Small benefits and specific exemptions

KRA’s guidance discusses a KES 5,000 monthly non-cash benefit threshold and separate treatment of meals, medical cover and pensions. It is not a blanket deduction to subtract from every car or house value. Identify the benefit’s specific provision before applying a general threshold.

Cheap loans need separate attention

Employer-provided low-interest loans may trigger fringe benefit tax with the employer as the taxpayer. The prescribed market rate can change. Do not automatically add every interest difference to employee PAYE using an old rate copied from a historical guide.

Keep the valuation evidence

  • Purchase or lease documents for vehicles.
  • Housing lease and the employee’s contribution, if any.
  • Records of benefit availability and private-use restrictions.
  • Policy and scheme details supporting exemptions.
  • A payroll calculation reconciling cash and taxable pay.

Explain benefits before an employee accepts a package: a perk can reduce cash take-home through additional PAYE. Reconcile the benefit on the P9 and retain the evidence supporting its value.

title: Finance Act Changes Affecting Kenyan Salaries: 2025–2026
content:
This guide replaces outdated claims about the Finance Bill 2025 with a dated account of the payroll issues employees need to check. A Bill, an enacted Act and an implementation notice are not interchangeable. Use the provision’s effective date when reviewing a payslip.

The PAYE bands were not invented in 2025

KRA’s current PAYE page continues to list the five rates introduced in July 2023: 10%, 25%, 30%, 32.5% and 35%. It lists resident personal relief of KES 2,400 monthly. The old article’s proposed 20% band and KES 2,880 personal relief should not be used for payroll.

Deductions and employer responsibility

Current payroll treatment recognises employee SHIF and Housing Levy as allowable deductions. The mortgage-interest and registered-pension ceilings are KES 30,000 monthly, subject to eligibility and the relevant limits. Do not also claim superseded SHIF or Housing Levy relief credits.

KRA’s October 2025 notice explains that employers must apply supported eligible deductions, reliefs and exemptions. Employees should supply the documents payroll needs. This is a compliance obligation, not a guarantee that every expense an employee requests qualifies.

February 2026 NSSF limits

The Year 4 notice raises the pensionable earnings ceiling to KES 108,000, with maximum employee NSSF of KES 6,480 and an equal employer contribution. This is a contribution change under the phased NSSF structure, not a new PAYE band. See the NSSF guide for its net-pay effect.

2026 gratuity conditions

KRA’s Finance Act 2026 summary specifies at least three continuous years of service under the relevant contract, or an extension of a three-year contract, and gratuity not exceeding 31% of the period’s emoluments for the exemption it describes. Do not rely on an older blanket statement that all gratuity is tax-free. See the terminal-dues guide and check the payment’s period and conditions.

The filing change from January 2027

KRA says individual return filing moves to the fourth month after year-end from 1 January 2027. For calendar-year individuals that means 30 April. Keep this distinct from the 30 June 2026 deadline for 2025 income and the employer’s monthly PAYE deadline.

What to do now

Check payroll’s NSSF period, supported reliefs and treatment of unusual payments. Prepare annual documents earlier for the next filing season. Preserve old-period calculations rather than applying new rules retrospectively. The dates in this guide explain different changes; they do not turn every 2026 payroll calculation into a 2027 calculation.

title: Kenya Tax Deadlines: PAYE and the 2027 Individual Filing Change
content:
Different taxes use different deadlines. In particular, PAYE uses the 9th day of the following month, Housing Levy uses the ninth working day, and individual annual returns have a separate filing timetable. Do not use a single “20th of the month” rule for everything.

Key payroll deadlines

ObligationDeadline / distinction
Employer PAYE return and payment9th of the following month
NSSF remittance9th of the following month under the 2026 notice
Housing LevyNinth working day after month-end
HELB deductions remittance15th of the following month
Turnover tax, if applicable20th of the following month

SHA remittance is a separate employer obligation; follow the current SHA employer instructions. Count working days correctly for Housing Levy and check specific official notices for any operational changes. Do not automatically shift a tax deadline to a date guessed from a weekend calendar.

Individual annual returns: distinguish the years

The 2025 calendar-year individual income return was due by 30 June 2026 under the earlier timetable. KRA’s Finance Act 2026 guidance states that, from 1 January 2027, individuals file by the last day of the fourth month after the year of income. For the calendar-year cycle, that is 30 April. Prepare 2026 records for the 2027 filing season on that basis and check KRA’s implementation notices.

A filing deadline is not automatically the payment deadline for every liability. Check any balance-of-tax and instalment obligations separately. Employer monthly PAYE filing also does not replace an employee’s annual income return.

Prepare the documents early

Collect P9s from each employer, insurance certificates, lender interest statements, pension evidence, exemption certificates and other income records as applicable. Check pre-filled amounts against those records. Do not submit a nil return merely because PAYE was already withheld: employment income is still income.

If you are late

File the correct return and establish the unpaid liability promptly. Penalties differ by tax and by whether the failure concerns filing, payment or deduction. The employer PAYE guide explains that regime; do not apply its penalty mechanically to an individual annual return.

A workable reminder system

Maintain separate entries for the payroll period, return due date, payment due date, acknowledgement and payment confirmation. Mark the obligation complete only when the required steps have succeeded. Retain screenshots and support references for system problems, but do not assume a support ticket automatically extends the legal deadline.

title: What Salary Do You Need to Live Comfortably in Nairobi?
content:
There is no single salary that guarantees a comfortable life in Nairobi. Household size, housing, commuting, debt and school costs can change the answer dramatically. Start with a monthly spending target and work backwards to the gross salary that funds it.

Use actual costs, not a universal lifestyle benchmark

List the rent you pay or a current quote for a property you would take. Add service charges, utilities and the deposit or moving costs separately. Use your own commute and food receipts. A neighbourhood name or an alleged “middle-class threshold” is not enough to establish your budget.

An illustrative monthly budget

CategoryExample KES
Rent and service charge25,000
Food and household supplies15,000
Transport8,000
Utilities and connectivity5,000
Health and personal costs4,000
Annual-cost sinking fund5,000
Savings and contingency8,000
Total net income target70,000

This is an arithmetic illustration, not a survey of Nairobi prices. Replace every line with your own figures. It excludes children’s fees, debt payments and dependants, which may materially increase the target. The purpose is to show how a budget becomes a net-income requirement.

Convert the target to gross salary

Under the standard resident employee assumptions used in our salary guides, KES 100,000 gross gives about KES 70,441.65 take-home after employee NSSF, SHIF, Housing Levy and PAYE. Personal payroll deductions can reduce that further. Use the net-to-gross calculator with your actual reliefs and deductions rather than adding an arbitrary percentage to the budget.

Include irregular costs

Divide known annual costs into monthly savings amounts: school terms, insurance renewals, travel, repairs or professional fees. Keep a separate contingency for costs whose amount or timing is uncertain. A budget that works only in months with no repairs or renewals is incomplete.

Check a change of job or home

A higher salary can be offset by a more expensive commute or lost employer benefits. Compare the net pay increase with those actual extra costs. Similarly, lower rent can be offset by transport, time or service charges. Use two complete budgets rather than comparing only headline salary or rent.

Keep assumptions visible

Date the quotes, record household size and distinguish essential costs from preferences. Review the budget when a real bill changes. Do not assume a fixed annual inflation rate, guaranteed investment return or universal savings percentage.

title: How a Second Job Is Taxed in Kenya
content:
Two jobs do not give you two independent annual personal-relief allowances. When employment income is reconciled for the year, the income and tax credits from both employers need to be considered together.

Why a shortfall can arise

Each employer may calculate withholding from the pay it knows about. If both start at the lowest bands or both apply personal relief, total withholding can be too low for the combined annual position. The outcome depends on the actual payroll treatment; it is not correct to say a second job always creates a tax bill.

Tell payroll about concurrent employment

Ask how secondary employment should be treated and which employer is granting personal relief. Keep the response and check the payslips. Where a deduction or exemption has an annual limit, do not assume each employer can independently grant the full allowance.

Illustrating the issue

If one job pays KES 80,000 and another pays KES 40,000, the combined gross cash income is KES 120,000. But simply adding two standalone net-pay calculator results does not prove the annual tax is correct. You must reconcile allowable deductions, benefits, the combined taxable income and tax already withheld.

Other contributions

Review NSSF, SHIF and Housing Levy under their own rules and payroll arrangements. Do not confuse an income-tax personal-relief issue with contribution limits. If both employers apply ceilings or deductions independently, ask the relevant authority or payroll teams how to reconcile the arrangement.

The annual return

Collect both P9s and verify the PIN, income and tax credit on each. Include other reportable income and check supported reliefs. Compare the final liability with tax already paid to establish any balance or overpayment. Retain documents from both employers even if one job ended partway through the year.

A freelance side job is different

If the second income is genuinely self-employment, it may involve business expenses, invoicing and withholding-tax credits rather than an employer PAYE calculation. The contract’s label alone does not determine the correct classification. See employment versus freelancing before treating contractor receipts as a second salary.

Check filing deadlines and job-change records when planning the reconciliation.

title: Tax on Terminal Dues in Kenya: Salary, Leave and Gratuity
content:
A final settlement can contain several payments with different tax treatment. Ask for an itemised breakdown rather than applying one percentage to the entire amount or assuming all terminal dues are tax-free.

Final salary and leave

Ordinary unpaid salary remains employment income. Leave pay and pay in lieu of notice need to be identified separately, including the period to which they relate. KRA’s lump-sum guidance explains allocation to relevant periods; its historical examples should not be copied with obsolete bands or relief amounts.

Gratuity: do not rely on a blanket exemption

The treatment has changed over time. For the exemption described in KRA’s Finance Act 2026 summary, the contract must cover at least three continuous years, or an extension of a three-year contract, and gratuity must not exceed 31% of the emoluments earned over the period. KRA’s summary presents these conditions as part of the 2026 changes.

Older guidance about the July 2025 exemption does not, on its own, settle a payment made under the newer rules. Give payroll the contract, service dates, gratuity formula and payment date, and ask it to identify the applicable provision. Where the payment straddles rule changes or the conditions are not met, get a documented calculation rather than assuming the whole payment is exempt.

Severance and retirement benefits are not interchangeable

A redundancy-related payment, contractual gratuity and a benefit paid from a pension scheme are different categories. Calling all of them “retirement money” does not give them identical treatment. Scheme benefits require their own eligibility and tax analysis; do not assume the gratuity rule applies to a pension withdrawal.

Questions for payroll

  • What are the gross amounts for salary, leave, notice, gratuity and any other component?
  • What period does each component relate to?
  • Which items are exempt, and under which provision?
  • How were taxable lump sums allocated and which rates were used?
  • What tax has already been paid for those periods?
  • What non-tax deductions or loan balances remain?

Keep the settlement documents

Retain the agreement, itemised calculation, final payslip and P9. Check that the bank amount reconciles to gross entitlements less deductions. If an employer corrects the settlement later, obtain revised supporting records for your return.

title: Company Car Benefit Tax in Kenya: Value Is Not Tax
metaTitle: Company Car Benefit Tax in Kenya: Value Is Not Tax | PAYE Calculator Kenya
metaDescription: Check the employer-owned car valuation rule and distinguish the taxable benefit from the additional PAYE and cash salary.
content:
A company car can increase taxable income even where your cash salary does not change. The benefit value and the PAYE on that value are different figures.

Employer-owned cars

The standard monthly valuation compares 2% of the vehicle’s initial cost with the prescribed benefit and uses the higher amount. For a car costing KES 3 million, the 2% calculation is KES 60,000. Confirm the applicable prescribed value before treating that as the final taxable benefit.

What it costs in PAYE

If the final extra taxable benefit is KES 60,000 and the whole amount falls in a 30% tax band, extra PAYE is KES 18,000. The employer does not add KES 60,000 cash to your salary, and the benefit value should not also be taken from cash as if it were a loan repayment.

Other arrangements

Leased vehicles and restrictions on private use require the relevant specific treatment. Keep the lease, cost record and use restrictions. Do not assume a percentage reduction without the supporting basis. The general small-benefit threshold is not a universal discount to subtract from every car benefit.

Check the full package

Ask payroll for the car benefit valuation, resulting taxable pay and additional PAYE. Compare the package with a cash alternative using both cash and non-cash value. An old guide may explain valuation but use outdated tax bands, so use current rates for current pay.

title: Turnover Tax on a Kenyan Side Hustle: Eligibility First
metaTitle: Turnover Tax on a Kenyan Side Hustle: Eligibility First | PAYE Calculator Kenya
metaDescription: Check the 1.5% turnover-tax regime, thresholds and professional-fee exclusions before applying it to side income.
content:
Turnover tax is not a default tax rate for every side hustle. First establish that the business and income qualify. Salary remains outside this business-turnover calculation.

Eligibility and exclusions

KRA lists eligible resident businesses with annual turnover above KES 1 million and no more than KES 25 million. It excludes rental income, management, professional and training fees, income subject to final withholding tax and non-residents. Professional freelancers should not assume they qualify because their revenue is within the limits.

The calculation

The published current rate is 1.5% of gross sales, with no deduction for expenses. KES 300,000 eligible monthly sales therefore gives KES 4,500 turnover tax. Compare that with actual profit to understand the cash burden; low turnover tax as a percentage of sales can still be a large share of a narrow margin.

Other obligations remain

KRA allows an election out of the regime by written notice, subject to the ordinary income-tax rules. Do not switch methods informally. VAT and other obligations need separate review; turnover tax is not a substitute for every business tax.

Filing and records

The return and payment are due by the 20th of the following month. Keep sales and purchase records, filing acknowledgements and payment references. Income subject to final turnover tax should not be taxed again as ordinary business income, but other reportable income may still require an annual return.

title: Non-Resident and Expatriate Employees: Kenyan PAYE Basics
metaTitle: Non-Resident and Expatriate Employees: Kenyan PAYE Basics | PAYE Calculator Kenya
metaDescription: Distinguish tax residence from nationality, check personal relief and identify cross-border issues before relying on a salary estimate.
content:
Being an expatriate does not automatically make someone non-resident for Kenyan tax. Equally, Kenyan nationality alone does not settle tax residence. Establish the relevant facts for the year before applying reliefs.

The residence tests

KRA’s definition includes a permanent home in Kenya with presence during the year. Without a permanent home, the alternatives include at least 183 days in the year, or presence in that year and each of the two preceding years averaging more than 122 days per year. Do not reduce the rule to a single 183-day test.

PAYE and personal relief

Kenya-source employment income can be taxable for non-residents. KRA’s PAYE guidance uses the individual bands for residents and non-residents, while resident personal relief is not granted to non-residents. A calculator that automatically subtracts KES 2,400 can therefore understate non-resident PAYE.

Cross-border work

An overseas payroll or foreign bank account does not by itself make income exempt. Work location, residence, the source of income and any applicable tax treaty need to be examined. Do not assume that foreign tax paid is automatically credited in full against Kenyan tax.

Records to prepare

Keep travel dates, employment contracts, payroll records, details of benefits and any foreign tax certificates. Ask payroll how it determined residence and the treatment of relocation, housing or travel benefits. Special exemptions have conditions and should not be applied solely because the employee is foreign.

title: How to Claim Overpaid PAYE in Kenya
metaTitle: How to Claim Overpaid PAYE in Kenya | PAYE Calculator Kenya
metaDescription: Reconcile P9s and supported reliefs, correct the return where necessary and submit an evidence-backed KRA refund claim.
content:
Overpaid PAYE can arise from a payroll error or a supported relief or deduction that was not applied. First establish the correct annual position; an unexpected payslip deduction does not by itself prove a refund is due.

Reconcile the documents

Collect the P9 from each employer, payslips, the filed return, tax-credit details and documents supporting the claim. Check insurance certificates, mortgage interest and pension records against what payroll already included. Do not claim the same deduction twice.

Correct and apply through the official process

Resolve incorrect payroll records or return figures using the appropriate correction procedure. KRA’s employee-refund guidance describes a separate refund application through iTax with supporting documents. Filing a return showing a credit does not necessarily complete that application.

What to expect

KRA may verify the figures and supporting evidence and account for outstanding tax liabilities. Keep the acknowledgement and follow up through official channels. Check the current statutory claim window for your period promptly; do not rely on an old article’s processing-time or interest promise.

If the claim is disputed

Request the written reason and check the formal response or objection route and its deadline. A support query is not necessarily a statutory objection. Keep the evidence and communications together until the matter is resolved.

title: Gross vs Net Salary in Kenya
metaDescription: Understand gross, basic and net salary in Kenya, see a KES 100,000 example and know what to ask before accepting a salary offer.
content:
Gross salary is your cash earnings before payroll deductions. Net salary is what remains after those deductions. If a Kenyan job offer says KES 100,000 gross a month, you should not budget on receiving KES 100,000 in your bank account.

The important question when comparing offers is which number the employer is quoting: basic salary, gross cash salary, net pay or the total employment package. These figures describe different things.

Four salary terms to separate

TermWhat it tells you
Basic salaryThe core contractual salary before separately listed allowances and variable pay.
Gross cash salaryCash earnings for the period before employee deductions.
Net salaryCash remaining after tax, contributions and other payroll deductions.
Total packageA wider offer figure that may include employer contributions and non-cash benefits. Ask for its components.

A KES 90,000 basic salary plus KES 10,000 of regular cash allowances can produce KES 100,000 gross. A KES 100,000 total package that includes employer costs may produce a lower gross cash salary. The headline amounts alone do not make the offers equivalent.

What does KES 100,000 gross leave you?

Our example assumes one resident employee, one job, a full month of regular cash salary and pensionable pay equal to gross pay. It uses the February 2026 NSSF limits and standard personal relief, with no benefits in kind, extra pension, mortgage deduction, insurance relief, disability exemption or personal repayments. Small payroll rounding differences are possible.

ItemMonthly KES
Gross cash salary100,000.00
Employee NSSF6,000.00
SHIF2,750.00
Employee Housing Levy1,500.00
PAYE19,308.35
Net salary70,441.65

The difference is KES 29,558.35, but that is not all income tax. It includes pension and health contributions and Housing Levy. See the full KES 100,000 salary breakdown for the tax calculation.

Why two people on the same gross can receive different amounts

A salary advance, HELB repayment or SACCO deduction can reduce the bank payment. Qualifying tax deductions and reliefs can change PAYE. A taxable non-cash benefit can affect tax without putting extra cash into the employee’s hands. Do not use a colleague’s bank deposit as proof that your payroll is wrong.

For budgeting, use the regular net figure after your own deductions. Keep occasional bonuses and expense reimbursements separate from the amount you rely on for rent, food and recurring bills.

Questions to ask before accepting an offer

  • Is the quoted salary basic, gross cash, guaranteed net or a total package?
  • Which allowances are fixed, and which depend on attendance or performance?
  • Are employer pension contributions additional to the quoted cash salary?
  • Can payroll provide a sample calculation using my circumstances?
  • If the offer promises net pay, what deductions does that promise cover?

Keep the written breakdown with your offer letter. If you are negotiating a specific bank payment, use the net-to-gross calculator and read how to work backwards from a take-home target.

Explore the salary breakdowns guide, or enter your actual gross pay in the PAYE calculator. For the separate figure used to calculate income tax, read taxable pay versus gross pay.

title: How to Read Your Kenyan Payslip
metaDescription: Read a Kenyan payslip line by line, reconcile earnings and deductions with your bank payment, and spot entries to query with payroll.
content:
Read a Kenyan payslip in three passes: confirm the pay period and earnings, check each deduction, then reconcile net pay with the money received. A payslip is a record of your employer’s calculation; the presence of a contribution on it does not by itself prove that the contribution reached the receiving institution.

Start with the month and the earnings

Check your name, employee number and payroll period before looking at the total. A first month, unpaid leave, an unpaid absence or a mid-month salary change can make the earnings different from a normal full month.

Separate basic salary from allowances, overtime, commission, bonus and arrears. Compare recurring amounts with your contract and variable amounts with the relevant approval or record. Ask what an unfamiliar earnings code means rather than assuming it is an extra benefit.

Know which figures are totals and which are calculations

Payslip labelHow to read it
Gross earningsStart here when checking cash earnings before deductions.
Taxable payA tax calculation figure; it is not another payment to add to gross.
PAYEThe employee’s income tax withheld through payroll.
NSSF, SHIF and Housing LevySeparate contributions, not extra names for PAYE.
Personal deductionsCheck repayments, savings and other deductions against your own records.
Net payThe resulting payment, subject to any separately explained payment arrangements.

An employer contribution shown for information is not automatically an employee deduction. Look at the column heading and ask payroll to explain any employer amount that appears to reduce your net pay.

Reconcile the bank payment

Try the simple reconciliation: gross cash earnings minus total employee cash deductions equals net pay. For example, KES 100,000 less KES 29,558.35 equals KES 70,441.65. The gross versus net guide sets out the assumptions behind those figures.

If the bank deposit differs, check whether a salary advance was already paid, the payment was split, or a reimbursement was paid separately. Do not add a non-cash car or housing benefit to the bank payment. Ask for a reconciliation that identifies each difference.

Check contributions beyond the payslip

Compare pension and health contribution records with the appropriate payroll months, allowing for the relevant remittance and posting process. NSSF’s 2026 notice separates the employee share from the employer share; a combined contribution is therefore not the same as the employee deduction on your payslip. Read the NSSF contribution guide before comparing the two.

For health contributions, use the SHIF guide to understand the deduction. Preserve any statement or payment reference supplied by payroll if you need to follow up a mismatch.

Send payroll a specific query

A useful request is: “Please explain the calculation of the [named deduction] on my [month] payslip, including the earnings base, rate and any adjustment carried forward. My expected figure is [amount] and the payslip shows [amount].” Attach the relevant payslip and supporting record through your employer’s secure channel.

Keep the reply and any corrected payslip. For a PAYE discrepancy, follow the wrong PAYE correction guide. Use the salary breakdowns hub and PAYE calculator as a cross-check with your own inputs.

title: Taxable Pay vs Gross Pay in Kenya
metaDescription: See why taxable pay differs from gross salary, which payroll entries affect each figure and how deductions differ from tax relief.
content:
Gross cash pay measures earnings before employee deductions. Taxable pay is the amount used to calculate income tax after relevant adjustments. Net pay is the cash left afterwards. Seeing three different figures on one payslip can be entirely correct.

This guide explains which column an item belongs in. For the full progressive-band calculation, use our step-by-step PAYE guide.

A bridge from gross pay to taxable pay

Start with taxable cash earnings, add any taxable value of non-cash benefits, then subtract qualifying deductions and apply any relevant exemption. The result is the income figure used for PAYE. The cash payment calculation follows a separate path.

Under KRA’s current guidance, SHIF and employee Housing Levy are allowable deductions. Registered pension contributions and qualifying mortgage interest can also qualify within the applicable limits and conditions. An item appearing under “deductions” on your payslip does not, on its own, make it an allowable tax deduction.

A KES 100,000 example

Our example assumes one resident employee, one job, a full month of regular cash salary and pensionable pay equal to gross pay. It uses the February 2026 NSSF limits and standard personal relief, with no benefits in kind, extra pension, mortgage deduction, insurance relief, disability exemption or personal repayments. Small payroll rounding differences are possible.

Calculation stepKES
Gross cash earnings100,000.00
Less employee NSSF6,000.00
Less SHIF2,750.00
Less employee Housing Levy1,500.00
Taxable pay89,750.00

KES 89,750 is a tax base, not your expected bank deposit. After calculating PAYE of KES 19,308.35, net cash is KES 70,441.65. The contributions already subtracted in arriving at taxable pay are also real cash deductions; do not deduct them twice when reconciling the final payment.

Classify a new payroll entry before changing your calculation

EntryQuestion to ask
A cash allowanceIs it taxable earnings, or is there a specific exclusion supported by records?
A car or housing benefitWhat taxable value has payroll calculated, and why?
A pension contributionHow much qualifies within the combined applicable limit?
A loan repayment or savings deductionDoes it simply reduce cash paid, rather than the tax base?
A tax reliefHas it been applied to calculated tax rather than subtracted from gross earnings?

This classification matters when comparing two months. A new personal repayment can lower your bank payment while leaving taxable pay unchanged. A newly recognised qualifying deduction can change taxable pay. A non-cash benefit may increase the taxable figure without increasing cash earnings.

A deduction is different from a relief

A deduction reduces the income on which tax is calculated. A relief reduces the resulting tax bill. Standard personal relief for a qualifying resident is KES 2,400 a month; it is not KES 2,400 of extra salary. For example, tax before relief of KES 21,708.35 becomes PAYE of KES 19,308.35 after that relief.

For the eligibility rules, see legal PAYE deductions and reliefs. For a benefit valuation, use the benefits-in-kind guide rather than treating every benefit as a cash allowance.

Which amount goes into the calculator?

Enter gross cash salary in the PAYE calculator, then supply the relevant benefit and deduction inputs. Entering taxable pay into a field labelled gross salary can cause contributions to be deducted again and produce a misleading result. The salary breakdowns hub shows how the figures fit together; the payslip guide helps you locate them on your own payroll record.
